lesson.title: Two Orbitals, One Straight Line: sp Hybridization
lesson.summary: When a central atom has only two electron domains, it mixes one s orbital and one p orbital into two sp hybrid orbitals pointing in exactly opposite directions, producing a perfectly linear 180 degree geometry.
lesson.body:
Orbital hybridization tells you that the number of hybrid orbitals an atom builds always matches its number of electron domains. The simplest possible case is two domains, and it produces the simplest possible hybridization: sp. To make two hybrid orbitals, an atom mixes exactly one s orbital with exactly one p orbital. The result is two sp hybrid orbitals, each carrying 50 percent s character and 50 percent p character, oriented at precisely 180 degrees from each other. This matches the linear electron domain geometry that VSEPR already assigns to any central atom with two domains and no lone pairs.

Mixing only one s orbital and one p orbital out of an atom's four valence orbitals leaves two p orbitals untouched. These leftover, unhybridized p orbitals sit perpendicular to each other and to the line formed by the two sp orbitals. They play no role in the sigma bonding framework built from the sp orbitals, but they are not wasted: whenever a sp hybridized atom is also part of a double or triple bond, these leftover p orbitals are exactly what forms the additional pi bonds, a connection explored fully once sigma and pi bonds are introduced.

Carbon dioxide is a clean worked example. The central carbon atom has two electron domains: one double bond to each oxygen, and no lone pairs. With two domains, carbon adopts sp hybridization, using its two sp orbitals to form the sigma bond half of each C-O double bond, and its two leftover p orbitals to form the pi bond half of each double bond. Because carbon has only two domains and no lone pairs to compress the angle, CO2 is perfectly linear, with an O-C-O bond angle of exactly 180 degrees, matching the 180 degree separation of the sp orbitals themselves.

Acetylene, C2H2, extends the same picture to a carbon-carbon triple bond. Each carbon in H-C triple bond C-H has two electron domains, one to its hydrogen and one to the other carbon, so both carbons are sp hybridized. Each carbon's two sp orbitals form sigma bonds, one to hydrogen and one to the other carbon, while each carbon's two leftover p orbitals form the two additional pi bonds of the triple bond. Every atom in acetylene lies on a single straight line, with all bond angles equal to 180 degrees.

sp hybridization is relatively rare compared to sp2 and sp3, because it requires a central atom with exactly two electron domains and therefore usually multiple bonds to accommodate a full octet. Beryllium chloride, BeCl2, is a classic textbook example of an sp hybridized central atom without any multiple bonding at all: beryllium has only two valence electrons, forms two single bonds to chlorine with no lone pairs, and the molecule is linear as a direct result of that sp geometry. In every case, the underlying rule is the same one introduced with linear geometry: two domains, no lone pairs, 180 degrees, now explained at the orbital level.
